title: The Trojan Horse
text:
For ten years the Greeks besieged Troy and could not take it. At last, on the advice of Odysseus, the craftsman Epeius built an enormous wooden horse. The best Greek warriors climbed inside it, and the rest of the army burned their camp and sailed away, though only as far as a nearby island, where they hid.

In the morning the Trojans found the beach empty and the great horse standing on it. Virgil's Aeneid tells how they argued over what to do. The priest Laocoon warned them that he feared the Greeks even when they brought gifts, and threw a spear into the horse's side. Then a Greek named Sinon, who had stayed behind on purpose, let himself be captured and told a convincing story: the horse was an offering to the goddess Athena, built so huge that the Trojans could not bring it into their city and win her favor. When two great serpents rose from the sea and killed Laocoon and his sons, the Trojans took it as a sign.

They pulled down part of their own walls to drag the horse inside and spent the night celebrating. While the city slept, Sinon let the warriors out. They opened the gates to the returning Greek army, and Troy was taken and burned.
lesson: When a direct assault fails for years, change the question from how to break in to how to be invited in. And be wary of gifts that require you to open your walls.
people: Odysseus, Epeius, Sinon, Laocoon, the Trojans
source: Homer, Odyssey, Books 4 and 8; Virgil, Aeneid, Book 2
caveat: Homer mentions the horse only briefly; the fuller story of Sinon and Laocoon comes from Virgil and other later poets.
